body:
Genetic information in living organisms

Every living organism contains genetic information that helps determine its inherited characteristics. In most organisms, this information is stored in deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). DNA consists of 2 complementary strands and contains information encoded in the sequence of 4 nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C).

A gene is a functional segment of genetic material that contributes to the production of a functional RNA or protein. Proteins perform many cellular functions and contribute to characteristics such as enzyme activity, growth and resistance to certain diseases. However, most characteristics depend on the interaction of several genes and environmental conditions.

A chromosome is an organised structure containing DNA and associated proteins. The genome is the complete genetic material of an organism. In humans, most cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. Mature red blood cells are an exception because they lack a nucleus.

A mutation is a change in genetic material. Mutations may occur naturally during DNA replication or because of environmental factors. Their effects can be beneficial, harmful or neutral, depending on the gene, the change and the circumstances.

What is genome editing?

Genome editing is a group of techniques used to make targeted changes to DNA sequences. An edit may remove, insert or alter genetic material.

Genome editing differs from merely reading a DNA sequence. DNA sequencing determines the order of bases; genome editing attempts to change that order. Editing may be used to study gene function, develop crop traits or treat selected genetic diseases.

How genome editing differs from traditional breeding

In conventional breeding, organisms with desirable characteristics are crossed, and offspring are selected over generations. This combines many inherited variations. In genetic engineering, selected genetic material can be introduced or modified more directly. Genome editing generally targets a particular DNA sequence, although an intended edit does not guarantee a successful or risk-free result.

ApproachMain actionImportant distinction
Conventional breedingCombines and selects inherited variationUsually changes many genetic combinations together
Recombinant DNA technologyCombines DNA from selected sourcesCan introduce a gene into a different organism
Genome editingTargets a particular DNA sequenceMay alter DNA without leaving foreign DNA in the final organism

These categories can overlap. A genome-edited organism has undergone deliberate genetic modification in the broad biological sense, but the legal classification of the resulting organism depends on the type of modification and the applicable regulations. Genome-edited and transgenic are therefore not interchangeable terms.

Prelims focus

  • DNA contains genetic information; a gene is a functional segment of genetic material.
  • A genome comprises an organism's complete genetic material.
  • Human somatic cells generally contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
  • Genome editing changes DNA; DNA sequencing reads its base sequence.
  • Trap: Genome editing does not necessarily require permanent insertion of a foreign gene.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class VIII, chapter Cell—Structure and Functions, sections 8.4–8.5 (GPSC Books compendium vol. 30, PDF pp. 94–96); NCERT, Biology, Class XII, chapter Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, section 11.1 (compendium vol. 35, PDF pp. 218–220); National Human Genome Research Institute, What Is Genome Editing?, Overview and In the Laboratory, consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: DNA, Genes and the Meaning of Genome Editing

body:
The origin of CRISPR

CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. In nature, CRISPR-associated systems form part of the defence mechanisms of certain bacteria and archaea against invading genetic material, including that of viruses.

Scientists adapted this biological system into a genome-editing tool. One widely used version is CRISPR-Cas9. It has 2 principal components: a guide RNA that helps locate the target DNA sequence and a Cas9 enzyme that can cut DNA.

The roles of guide RNA and Cas9

The guide RNA contains a sequence designed to recognise a complementary region of target DNA. The Cas9 protein is a nuclease, meaning an enzyme capable of cutting nucleic acids. The guide RNA directs Cas9 towards the intended location. Cas9 also requires a suitable nearby DNA recognition feature called a PAM sequence.

Once the target is recognised, Cas9 can produce a break in both DNA strands. The cell's own repair machinery then responds. The final genetic change depends on how the break is repaired.

Why DNA repair matters

  • Repair that produces small insertions or deletions: Small changes can disrupt a gene so that it no longer produces a functional product. This is commonly called a gene knockout.
  • Repair using a suitable DNA template: Under appropriate conditions, a cell may use a supplied sequence to make a more specific change, including replacement of a faulty sequence.

The first outcome is often easier to obtain than precise replacement. An accurate DNA cut does not by itself guarantee that the desired repair will occur.

CRISPR identifies the target; Cas9 cuts the DNA; the cell repairs the break. These are different functions. Guide RNA is not itself the DNA-cutting enzyme.

Scientific importance

CRISPR-Cas9 made many targeted genetic changes easier to design than earlier approaches that required a separately engineered DNA-binding protein for each target. It is useful for studying gene function, improving selected agricultural traits and developing medical treatments.

The 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna for the development of a method for genome editing. Their contribution is a historical scientific fact, not the same as claiming that they discovered DNA or invented every form of genetic engineering.

Important limitations

CRISPR is powerful but not perfectly precise in every situation. It may sometimes act at an unintended DNA site, and the cell may repair a targeted break in an unexpected way. A successful laboratory edit must therefore be assessed for both its intended result and possible harmful changes.

Prelims focus

  • CRISPR originated from microbial defence mechanisms.
  • Guide RNA helps identify the DNA target.
  • Cas9 is a DNA-cutting enzyme.
  • DNA repair determines the genetic result after a Cas9 cut.
  • The 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna.
  • Trap: The guide RNA locates the target; it does not itself cut DNA.

[Sources: National Human Genome Research Institute, How Does Genome Editing Work?, CRISPR section, consulted 5 November 2026; National Institute of General Medical Sciences, What Is CRISPR?, October 2024, CRISPR in the Laboratory; NobelPrize.org, The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020, press release dated 7 October 2020.]

pictures.alt: Guide RNA targets complementary DNA, Cas9 cuts both strands, and cellular repair may cause a gene knockout or a targeted sequence change.
pictures.caption: Guide RNA directs Cas9 to a DNA target, after which cellular repair determines the final edit.

title: CRISPR-Cas9: How Targeted DNA Editing Works

body:
CRISPR is not the only editing technology

Several technologies can identify particular DNA sequences and enable genetic changes. Their common purpose is targeted alteration of genetic information, but they differ in how they recognise DNA and produce an edit.

ToolBasic principleKey distinction
CRISPR-Cas9Guide RNA directs a Cas enzyme to DNATarget selection mainly depends on RNA sequence design
Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs)Engineered proteins recognise DNA and cut itUses specially designed DNA-binding proteins
TALENsEngineered DNA-binding proteins are linked to nucleasesUses a different protein-based recognition system
Base editingChanges selected DNA bases without a conventional double-strand cutUseful for certain small sequence changes

Not every tool can make every desired change. The choice depends on the DNA target, the type of edit and the cell being treated. For prelims, the central distinction is RNA-guided recognition in CRISPR-Cas9 versus engineered protein-based recognition in ZFNs and TALENs.

The problem of delivering editing tools

An editing system must reach the relevant cells before it can work. DNA, RNA or proteins do not automatically enter every target tissue. Delivery is therefore an important part of both experimental and medical genome editing.

Two broad approaches

  • Ex vivo editing: Cells are obtained from a patient or donor, modified outside the body, assessed and then introduced into the recipient. Edited blood-forming stem cells provide an important medical example.
  • In vivo editing: The editing system is delivered directly into the body to reach the intended cells or tissue.

Possible delivery methods include modified viral vectors and non-viral carriers such as lipid nanoparticles. These are delivery systems, not separate kinds of genome editing. A vector that carries genetic material does not necessarily become part of the recipient's chromosomes.

What can go wrong?

Off-target effects occur when an editing system changes DNA at an unintended location. Unintended on-target effects occur when the correct region is targeted but the resulting change is larger or different from the intended edit. These are distinct risks.

Other concerns include unsuccessful delivery, effects on the wrong cell type, immune reactions to delivery materials and mosaicism, in which some cells carry an edit while others do not. The significance of these problems varies with the organism, tissue and intended application.

A technique may be highly accurate in recognising DNA but still give an undesirable result because DNA repair, delivery or the biology of the target cells behaves unexpectedly. Precision is therefore not identical to safety.

How safety is judged

Safety assessment considers whether the intended DNA change occurred, whether unintended changes arose, whether the desired biological effect was obtained and whether adverse consequences appear over an appropriate observation period. In medical applications, benefits must be weighed against risks for the particular patient and disease.

Prelims focus

  • ZFNs and TALENs use engineered DNA-binding proteins.
  • CRISPR-Cas9 uses guide RNA for target recognition.
  • Ex vivo means cells are modified outside the body; in vivo means editing takes place inside the body.
  • Off-target effects involve unintended DNA locations.
  • Unintended on-target effects occur at the intended location.
  • Trap: Viral vectors and lipid nanoparticles are delivery methods, not editing enzymes.

[Sources: National Human Genome Research Institute, How Does Genome Editing Work?, sections on zinc-finger nucleases, TALENs and CRISPR, consulted 5 November 2026; National Human Genome Research Institute, What Is Genome Editing?, Technical Barriers; National Institute of General Medical Sciences, What Is CRISPR?, October 2024.]

pictures.alt: Ex vivo editing removes cells for modification and assessment before transfer; in vivo delivery brings the editing system to target cells inside the body.
pictures.caption: Ex vivo editing modifies cells outside the body; in vivo editing acts within the body.

title: Genome Editing Tools, Delivery Methods and Risks

body:
The distinction depends on the cells affected

Human cells can be divided broadly into somatic cells, which form the tissues of the body, and germline cells, which are involved in the formation of future generations. The difference matters because a genetic change in a body cell is not ordinarily transmitted to children, whereas a change affecting reproductive genetic material may be inherited.

FeatureSomatic editingHeritable germline editing
Cells involvedNon-reproductive body cellsReproductive cells or embryos whose edits can enter the germline
Main objectiveBenefit the treated individualAlter genetic information that may reach future generations
InheritanceNot ordinarily passed to offspringMay be passed to offspring
Ethical concernPatient safety and consentSafety, consent and effects on future generations

Editing an embryo does not automatically produce a uniform change in every cell. If only some cells are changed, the resulting organism may be mosaic. Whether a change is inherited depends on whether it reaches reproductive cells.

Genome editing and gene therapy are related but different

Gene therapy attempts to treat or prevent disease by changing how genetic material functions in a patient's cells. Some gene therapies add a functioning gene or change gene expression without editing the original DNA sequence. Genome-editing therapy deliberately modifies a DNA sequence. Thus, genome editing can be one type of gene therapy, but not all gene therapy uses genome editing.

Some inherited diseases result mainly from a change in a single gene. Such disorders may be suitable targets for specific genetic treatments. However, a disease involving many genes, environmental factors or damage across several organs is generally more difficult to correct by changing a single DNA sequence.

Why heritable editing raises special ethical concerns

A person receiving somatic therapy can, in principle, give informed consent after understanding its possible benefits and risks. Future generations affected by heritable germline editing cannot provide such consent. Moreover, an unintended inherited change could persist beyond the initially treated individual.

Questions also arise about unequal access to expensive treatments, pressure to select non-medical characteristics, possible discrimination against people with disabilities and the distinction between treating serious disease and attempting human enhancement.

International governance

The World Health Organization published Human Genome Editing: Recommendations on 12 July 2021. It emphasised strong oversight, responsible research, transparency, registration and international cooperation. These recommendations are an international governance framework; they are not themselves a uniform law automatically applicable in every country.

Somatic editing concerns the treated person's body cells. Heritable germline editing concerns changes that may be transmitted to descendants. The possibility of inheritance, rather than the editing tool alone, creates the central distinction.

Prelims focus

  • Somatic genome editing is ordinarily non-heritable.
  • Heritable germline editing may affect future generations.
  • Gene therapy does not always involve direct DNA editing.
  • Mosaicism means that not all cells carry the same genetic change.
  • WHO issued human genome-editing recommendations on 12 July 2021.
  • Trap: Editing a patient's blood cells does not mean the patient's children inherit the edit.

[Sources: National Human Genome Research Institute, What Is Genome Editing?, Treating Disease and Ethical Concerns, consulted 5 November 2026; World Health Organization, Human Genome Editing: Recommendations, 12 July 2021, Overview and governance recommendations.]

pictures.alt: Somatic edits are ordinarily not inherited; germline edits may pass to offspring. Mosaicism means only some cells carry the edit.
pictures.caption: Somatic changes remain within the treated individual, while heritable germline changes may reach descendants.

title: Somatic and Germline Editing: Inheritance, Medicine and Ethics
